---
title: "Solution: Distance Measures and k-Means Clustering"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(factoextra)

source("courses/bdat-602/_teacher/resources/datasets/simulate_bdat602_data.R")
health_data <- simulate_bdat602(n = 500000, seed = 602)
```

## Task 1: Prepare and scale the clustering features

```{r task1-sample}
set.seed(602)
health_sub <- health_data |>
  filter(!is.na(bmi), !is.na(income)) |>
  slice_sample(n = 50000)

cluster_vars <- c("age", "bmi", "income", "premium",
                  "num_chronic_conditions", "num_claims",
                  "claim_amount", "support_calls",
                  "customer_rating", "app_logins_monthly")
```

```{r task1-transform-scale}
signed_log <- function(x) sign(x) * log1p(abs(x))

health_scaled <- health_sub |>
  select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  mutate(
    income       = signed_log(income),
    claim_amount = log1p(claim_amount)
  ) |>
  scale() |>
  as.data.frame()

colMeans(health_scaled) |> round(3)  # all ~0
apply(health_scaled, 2, sd) |> round(3)  # all ~1
```

## Task 2: Distance measures on the first five observations

```{r task2-euclidean}
d_euclid <- dist(health_scaled[1:5, ], method = "euclidean")
print(round(as.matrix(d_euclid), 3))
```

```{r task2-manhattan}
d_manhattan <- dist(health_scaled[1:5, ], method = "manhattan")
print(round(as.matrix(d_manhattan), 3))

# Manhattan distances are consistently larger than Euclidean distances because
# Manhattan sums absolute differences while Euclidean takes a square root of
# squared differences — the square root compresses large differences.
# The RANKING of pairwise distances can differ: if two policyholders differ
# greatly on one feature and little on others, Euclidean distance will be less
# affected by those small differences than Manhattan (which adds them linearly).
# This matters when some features have naturally higher variance even after scaling.
```

## Task 3: Elbow plot — choose k

```{r task3-elbow}
set.seed(602)
fviz_nbclust(
  health_scaled, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 10, nstart = 10
) +
  labs(title = "Elbow Method: Choosing Optimal k",
       x = "Number of Clusters k",
       y = "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r task3-choose-k}
# The elbow typically appears at k = 4 for this dataset:
# WCSS drops steeply from k=1 to k=4, then the marginal reduction per additional
# cluster flattens. k=4 balances compactness with interpretability.
chosen_k <- 4
```

## Task 4: Fit k-means, profile, and label clusters

```{r task4-fit}
set.seed(602)
km_fit <- kmeans(health_scaled,
                 centers = chosen_k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)

cat("Variance explained:",
    round(km_fit$betweenss / km_fit$totss * 100, 1), "%\n")
cat("Cluster sizes:", km_fit$size, "\n")
```

```{r task4-profile}
health_sub$cluster <- factor(km_fit$cluster)

cluster_profile <- health_sub |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(
    n           = n(),
    avg_age     = round(mean(age), 1),
    avg_bmi     = round(mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    avg_income  = round(mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), 0),
    avg_claims  = round(mean(num_claims), 2),
    pct_smoker  = round(mean(smoker) * 100, 1),
    pct_fraud   = round(mean(fraud_flag) * 100, 1),
    pct_churned = round(mean(churned) * 100, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_claims))

print(cluster_profile)
```

```{r task4-visualise}
fviz_cluster(
  km_fit,
  data         = health_scaled,
  geom         = "point",
  ellipse      = TRUE,
  ellipse.type = "convex",
  alpha        = 0.3,
  palette      = c("#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#984EA3"),
  ggtheme      = theme_minimal(),
  main         = "k-Means Clusters (k = 4): PCA Projection"
)
```

```{r task4-labels}
# Typical labels (exact cluster numbers depend on random seed):
# Cluster with highest avg_claims and avg_bmi:
#   "Elderly High-Utilisation" — oldest, most chronic conditions, most claims
# Cluster with highest pct_smoker and elevated avg_bmi:
#   "High-Risk Smoker Segment" — moderate age, high BMI, elevated fraud rate
# Cluster with lowest avg_age and avg_claims:
#   "Young Healthy Low-Risk" — youngest, fewest claims, lowest fraud rate
# Remaining cluster:
#   "Middle-Aged Moderate-Risk" — mid-range on all metrics, moderate income
#
# These segments guide: risk-adjusted pricing, targeted wellness programmes,
# churn prevention for the low-risk young segment, and fraud screening for
# the high-BMI smoker group.
```
